title: Best-Selling Ballads and their Pictures in Seventeenth-Century England
abstract: This article examines the woodcut pictures that appeared on best-selling ballads published in London during the seventeenth century. One hundred and twenty-five of the period’s top ballads are identified using a range of criteria and a selection of these publications is then studied in multiple editions. It is argued that the dismissive attitude to the pictures that has often been adopted by scholars is urgently in need of revision. The woodcut pictures were an integral component of the genre and deserve to studied closely. Publishers and printers were keenly aware of the importance of the pictures and put considerable thought into their preparation and placement. Thus, the pictures helped to generate meaning for contemporary consumers, and the re-use of old woodcuts on new ballads set up interesting connections between different publications. Overall, it is argued that there was a sophisticated web of reference and association at work within the pictorial culture of balladry.

narrative:
Short impact summary

Christopher Marsh’s Best-Selling Ballads and their Pictures in Seventeenth-Century England shows clear scholarly uptake. The article has been cited 19 times and has 19 documented downstream reuses, with later work drawing on its argument that the woodcut images on broadside ballads were integral to the genre rather than incidental decoration.

Full narrative

Published in Past & Present in 2016, this article has developed a focused but recognizable research footprint in historical, literary, and musicological scholarship. The citation record shows 19 citing works, and the reuse record matches that total, indicating that the article’s core claim has been repeatedly taken up rather than merely noted in passing. The strongest concentration appears in book chapters, especially within Cambridge University Press volumes, which suggests that the article has become part of broader synthetic discussions about ballads, performance, and music history.

The surrounding citing landscape points to a coherent thematic reception. Later works most often engage the article through musicology and the history of performance, but the concepts attached to the citing literature also include ballad studies, literature, and cultural history. This fits the article’s own intervention: a reassessment of the pictorial woodcuts that accompanied seventeenth-century ballads, and a challenge to older dismissive interpretations of those images. Rather than being treated as marginal ornament, the pictures have been absorbed into later scholarship as evidence relevant to representation, narration, and popular print culture.

The pattern of reuse is also institutionally concentrated. Most citing works come from the United Kingdom and from education-sector authors, with a particularly strong cluster at the University of East Anglia. That concentration is consistent with a specialist scholarly conversation in adjacent fields rather than a diffuse public profile. There is no evidence in the record of social-media or news-style attention, and the scite and event-data signals are empty, so the article’s impact is best understood through formal academic citation and reuse.

The work is also available through multiple open repository instances, which may have supported discoverability and reuse. Overall, the record shows a durable specialist influence: the article has become a source that later scholars cite when discussing ballads, performance, representation, and the visual culture of early modern print. Its impact is concentrated rather than broad, but the citation and reuse evidence together indicate sustained scholarly value.
